projects.name: DEFTECHLINK
projects.description: DEFTECHLINK is a startup platform connecting defense innovation opportunities with industry, academia, and government partners. I built the entire frontend from scratch, integrating RESTful APIs, implementing authentication flows, setting up Stripe payments for onboarding, and ensuring a responsive, accessible, and polished user interface.

caseStudy.role: Lead Full Stack Developer & UI/UX Designer
caseStudy.summary: DEFTECHLINK is a startup platform that connects defense innovation opportunities across industry, academia, and government. I joined as a Frontend Developer and quickly expanded into a Lead Full Stack Developer & UI/UX Designer, helping build the platform from the ground up alongside one other engineer. I led the frontend experience while contributing across the full stack, from wireframing and branding to API integrations, authentication, and Stripe-powered onboarding.
caseStudy.problem: Organizations entering or expanding within the defense industry often rely on fragmented resources for opportunities, funding, networking, and market intelligence. DEFTECHLINK aimed to centralize these resources into a single platform that felt modern, trustworthy, and intuitive despite the complexity of the domain.
caseStudy.approach: My process always began with understanding the problem before writing code. I created low-fidelity wireframes in Figma to validate navigation and user flows, using them as the blueprint for development. Although the final product evolved significantly beyond these early concepts, they established the structure that shaped the application. Because the platform served the defense industry, I also invested time learning defense terminology, procurement workflows, and the competitive landscape so the user experience reflected the needs of our audience.

decisions.title: Wireframe the whole product before high fidelity
decisions.reason: The portal spanned seven+ distinct screens and workflows. Creating low-fidelity wireframes first allowed me to validate navigation, information hierarchy, and user flows early before investing time in detailed designs or implementation.

decisions.title: Build a scalable content management system
decisions.reason: I developed a role-based content management system that supported both administrative workflows and learner experiences. Administrators could create rich-text resources, upload videos, manage metadata, schedule publications, organize content into courses and collections, attach downloadable templates, and analyze user feedback through built-in analytics. This architecture allowed content teams to manage educational resources without developer intervention while giving learners a structured and intuitive way to discover and engage with content.

decisions.title: Balance speed with scalability
decisions.reason: With only two engineers building the platform, every technical decision needed to support rapid development without sacrificing maintainability. I focused on creating reusable components, consistent design patterns, and clean integrations so we could continue shipping features as the product evolved.

caseStudy.iterationIntro: As DEFTECHLINK's product direction evolved, I continuously refined the landing page experience to better align with changing business goals and user needs. Across three iterations, the feature section shifted from presenting all capabilities equally to establishing a clearer hierarchy around the platform's core value, helping users better understand the product and discover the workflows most relevant to them.

design.label: From Structure to Visual Direction
design.caption: Early low-fidelity wireframes helped establish the landing page structure, content hierarchy, and user flow. From there, I refined individual sections into high-fidelity designs by applying the DEFTECHLINK brand identity, visual language, and product direction.

design.label: Platform Architecture & User Flows
design.caption: Early wireframes mapping the core platform experience across the dashboard, opportunities, teammate marketplace, learning hub, funding, and events. Defining the overall structure upfront helped establish consistent navigation patterns and create a foundation for development.

design.label: Initial Product Direction
design.caption: The first iteration introduced DEFTECHLINK's core platform capabilities. As the product evolved, it became clear that presenting every feature with equal weight made it difficult for users to grasp the platform's primary value.

design.label: Prioritizing Opportunities as the Core Value
design.caption: As DEFTECHLINK expanded, we identified opportunities as the platform's primary value proposition. I redesigned the feature hierarchy to lead with opportunity discovery, then restructured the supporting features around the user's journey into the defense ecosystem.

design.label: Improving Understanding & Engagement
design.caption: The third iteration focused on reducing cognitive load and helping users understand the platform before exploring it. I streamlined the feature presentation, cut unnecessary scrolling, and introduced product demonstrations to communicate functionality more effectively.

caseStudy.outcome: The result was a production-ready platform built from the ground up, where the brand experience, marketing site, onboarding flow, and authenticated application shared a consistent design language. Working alongside one other engineer, I helped establish the frontend architecture, reusable design patterns, and user experiences that allowed DEFTECHLINK to continue expanding as the product evolved. The platform provided a foundation for connecting defense organizations with opportunities, resources, and collaboration tools through a modern, accessible, and intuitive experience.

projects.name: MORPH
projects.description: Morph is a browser-based file transformation toolkit for converting, compressing, and managing digital files. I designed and developed the application using React and WebAssembly-powered tools, building an intuitive interface with real-time feedback, local file processing, and a seamless workflow without requiring accounts or uploads.

caseStudy.summary: Morph is a file transformation toolkit designed to simplify everyday tasks like converting, compressing, and merging files through a clean, intuitive interface. While many existing tools accomplish these tasks, they often interrupt workflows with advertisements, aggressive paywalls, confusing navigation, or unnecessary account requirements. Morph was built to provide a faster, more thoughtful experience that prioritizes usability, accessibility, and efficiency for students, designers, developers, and anyone working with digital files.
caseStudy.problem: File conversion has become an everyday task, yet many existing tools introduce unnecessary friction through advertisements, usage limits, account requirements, or inconsistent user experiences. As both a UI/UX designer and software developer, I frequently found myself switching between multiple websites just to compress images, convert formats, or merge documents. Rather than continuing to adapt to fragmented workflows, I set out to design a single tool that felt fast, approachable, and enjoyable to use.
caseStudy.approach: Rather than designing around individual conversion tools, I approached Morph as a unified file utility. Every interaction was designed to minimize friction, from drag-and-drop uploads and batch processing to automatically surfacing the most relevant conversion options based on the uploaded files. My goal was to make common tasks feel effortless while maintaining a consistent visual language across converting, compressing, and merging workflows.

decisions.title: Build around workflows, not file formats
decisions.reason: Rather than organizing Morph around dozens of individual conversion tools, I structured the experience around the tasks users are trying to accomplish: converting, merging, and compressing files. This simplified navigation while creating a foundation that can naturally expand as new file types and capabilities are introduced.

decisions.title: Design for scalability from day one
decisions.reason: Although Morph began as an image conversion tool, I designed the information architecture to support future file types and workflows. Organizing features into reusable categories rather than individual converters allows the product to grow without requiring a complete redesign.

decisions.title: Keep users informed at every step
decisions.reason: Rather than treating file conversion as a simple upload-and-download interaction, I designed Morph to provide continuous feedback throughout the entire process. Users can view processing progress, preview the converted file, and compare the original and optimized file sizes alongside the percentage saved.

caseStudy.iterationIntro: As Morph grew from a single image converter into a broader file transformation toolkit, I refined the conversion experience to keep it simple as the number of supported formats increased. Across two iterations, the interface moved from asking users to choose a conversion path upfront to detecting the uploaded file and surfacing only the relevant options, then reorganized those options around the destination format so the navigation could scale without becoming harder to scan.

design.label: Initial concept wireframes for the Convert workflow
design.caption: Early Figma wireframes exploring the Convert experience in both light and dark themes. The concepts define the primary interface, conversion menu, upload workflow, and completed queue, including conversion metadata such as original size, converted size, files processed, and storage savings.

design.label: Evolution of the Convert interface
design.caption: Evolution of the Convert interface from initial concepts to the final implementation. The first image is the wireframe, the second is a high-fidelity design, and the third is the final implementation. The final design simplified the interface, reduced cognitive load, and improved usability while maintaining a consistent visual language across all workflows.

design.label: Shifting to a File-First Workflow
design.caption: The initial interface assumed a conversion path before the user provided a file, which meant the displayed conversion wasn’t always relevant. By detecting the uploaded file type automatically, Morph adapts the available conversion options in real time. This change minimizes unnecessary interaction, reduces cognitive load, and keeps users focused on their primary task.

design.label: Simplifying Conversion Navigation
design.caption: As Morph expanded to support additional file formats, listing every individual conversion quickly became difficult to scan. Rather than presenting options like PNG → WebP, JPG → WebP, and GIF → WebP separately, I reorganized the interface around the destination format. Grouping conversions as To WebP, To PNG, or To JPG reduced visual clutter while creating a navigation system that can scale naturally as more formats are added.

caseStudy.outcome: Morph demonstrates the way I enjoy building products by identifying a frustrating everyday workflow, designing a thoughtful solution, iterating on feedback, and shipping a polished experience. Rather than recreating existing converter websites, I focused on removing the friction they often introduce through confusing navigation, unnecessary decisions, and inconsistent user experiences. As the project evolved, so did the product itself. What began as a simple image converter grew into a unified file transformation toolkit built around user workflows instead of individual file formats. Designing with scalability in mind allowed new capabilities to be introduced without sacrificing the simplicity, consistency, and ease of use that defined the experience from the start.
